Initially, I added a check on the log-determinant value so that we can catch degenerate cases where eigenvalues are so small that logdet == -np.inf. The check is `if np.isinf(logdet)`, which also include the case "log-det is too big".
Regarding the eigenvalues you gave, if you have a large number of features, it could be that the log-det goes to infinity. Could that be?
Thanks, I'll have a look later.

hm det is `-inf`.
The `covariance` matrix used there is indeed singular. I'm not sure where that happens, though, as I'm not familiar with the algorithm. The data that comes in is definitely not singular. I'll try to create a self-contained example.

The `covariance` variable in MinCovDet code can be the covariance of a subsample (i.e. `np.dot(data[mask].T, data[mask]`) for a given mask). Maybe your data are organized in subsets so that subsampling your original data leads you to work with singular covariances?
(example of such a case: a dataset made of two clusters having each a badly-scaled "intra covariance" matrix.)
thanks, that's what I was thinking about. I'll have a closer look at my data again.

Hm I can't see something like that.
It picked a 300 samples big subset (in 200 dimensions) and that seems to be singular.
Should I upload the data set to a gist?

Is there any way to deal with this issue?

I can have a look at the data, hoping that I will be able to fall in the same state (because the algorithm uses a random subsampling scheme. Did you seed it by the way?)

One strong hypothese going with the use of EllipticEnvelope/MinCovDet, is that your data must look like a n-dimensional ellipsoid. If it is not the case, many weird things can happen, without us being able to catch anything with a good explaination.
I think my strategy will consist in trying to perform some projection pursuit algorithm on your data in order to see if clusters appear (the data would therefore not be gaussian distributed for sure). Alternatively, I may try to perform some kind of clustering (Ward? KNN?).

Thanks for investigating. My data set is [here](https://gist.github.com/3755501).
Maybe I should switch to one class svm for more robust outlier detection then...
I usually use it as preprocessing for kmeans ^^

>    Maybe I should switch to one class svm for more robust outlier detection
>    then...

OCSVM is not a good outlier detection method, it is a good novelty
detection method. In other words, it needs a pure dataset, without
outliers, for training. I does work often as an outlier detection method,
but it is hard to control.

If you are using this as a preprocessing step to k-means, I wonder if
DBScan wouldn't be useful.

Our implementation is slow, but maybe this is fixeable.

> OCSVM is not a good outlier detection method, it is a good novelty detection method.

But if you assume that the outliers do not change the data shape too much, OCSVM can still be useful. Also, OCSVM can still track gross outliers like in scikit-learn's example: http://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/covariance/plot_outlier_detection.html .

For non-parametric outlier detection, density estimation seems to be the most relevant method, but I do not think you can directly use sklearn and its API to do so. You would need use a density estimator such as Parzen Windows and then remove a given proportion of observations (the one that fall in the less dense regions).
Why do you think there is an API issue with this approach? In how far is it different from the `EllipticEnvelope`?

I mean that no ParzenWindows object exists in the scikit-learn. In the case we had, it would be easy to have it inherit from the OutlierDetectionMixin and give it a decision function that could trim the data according the the `contamination` parameter. But this would need further developments and that is why I said it was not currently possible with scikit-learn.

`EllipticEnvelope` tries to find an ellipsoid that encompass a given proportion of the data, thought to be the inliers. It assumes that the observations are distributed according to a Gaussian distribution (or, at lest, a unimodal, symmetric distribution). A density estimator would point the more densely populated regions, whatever their distribution and shape, making it possible to adapt to various data configurations.

Yeah sure, it's not implemented yet. And it could be quite inefficient :-/
Maybe if we use a ball-tree and do a cut-off. But then we still need the bandwidth...

Maybe for my case it would be good enough to use a standard Gaussian fit. That seems to be more robust than the robust one ;)

>    Why do you think there is an API issue with this approach?

It's not an API issue, it's just that the KDE (Kernel Density Estimator)
of scipy does not expose the estimator API of scikit-learn.

That said, it also doesn't scale well if there are a lot of training
points. I might be useful to write a KDE for outlier detection based on
our KNN. It shouldn't be too hard. It would probably work quite well in
terms of outlier detection for datasets that lie in a low dimensional
manifold.
One could use a nearest-neighbor based non-parametric entropy estimate.... but that would probably count as somewhat experimental ;)

>    Yeah sure, it's not implemented yet. And it could be quite inefficient :-/
>    Maybe if we use a ball-tree and do a cut-off.

Yes, that's a mandatory step. Elsewhere things are just too slow.

>    Maybe for my case it would be good enough to use a standard Gaussian fit.

Depends on the shape of your data, and the n / p ratio.

>    One could use a nearest-neighbor based non-parametric entropy estimate....

Forget about the entropy, and keep the nearest-neighbor idea... you get
something close to the Parzen estimate that we are discussing. I think
that this is a good tool in many situations.
Do you have a reference?
